Explain the mechanism of temporal summation, Temporal summation occurs when a single presynaptic neuron fires repeated short-duration impulses in rapid succession. Enumerate the main properties of the stretch reflex. « It is a somatic spinal deep reflex. « Shows some properties of polysynaptic + Adequate stimulus is muscle stretch. reflexes such as reciprocal innervation, « Receptors are muscle spindles. summation, and rebound. « Center is spinal motor neurons. « Static type is slowly adapting; dynamic type « It is the only monosynaptic reflex in the body. is rapidly adapting. « Reaction time is short (19-24 msec). * Static type is present in all muscles, especially « Central delay is about 0.5-0.9 msec. antigravity muscles. ¢ It has no afterdischarge (no interneurons). * Static type is inhibited by overstretch through « Highly localized: occurs in the stretched the inverse stretch reflex. muscle. * Contraction is jerky in the dynamic type and smooth in the static type. Facilitates muscle tone, enhances postural reflexes, and helps maintain equilibrium by acting on alpha motor neurons. What happens to muscle tone if the lateral reticulospinal tract is overactive? Muscle tone decreases due to inhibition of gamma motor neuron activity. Describe the effect of lesioning both ventral and lateral vestibulospinal tracts. Disturbed postural control, loss of equilibrium, and hypotonia due to reduced facilitation of alpha motor neurons. Explain the effect of a lesion in the internal capsule on motor function. Causes contralateral hemiplegia because the internal capsule contains tightly packed corticospinal fibers for the whole body. Explain the effect of a unilateral spinal cord lesion above the brachial plexus. Causes ipsilateral spinal hemiplegia, affecting motor function on the same side. Effect of lesion in area 4 of the motor cortex. Causes contralateral monoplegia, depending on the extent and location of damage. Effect of lesion in the corticobulbar tract affecting the facial nerve. Causes contralateral lower facial paralysis, sparing the upper face due to bilateral input. Effect of bilateral lesion below the brachial and above the lumbosacral plexus. Results in paraplegia—paralysis of both lower limbs. Why is the upper face spared in unilateral corticobulbar lesions? Because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical innervation, while the lower part receives contralateral only. Why is partial recovery possible in hemiplegia? Due to the presence of uncrossed fibers (e.g., from the ventral and ipsilateral corticospinal tracts), which innervate muscles for functions like speech, breathing, etc. Why is the internal capsule highly vulnerable to lesions? Because it contains densely packed descending fibers from the cortex, making it a major site of motor signal transmission. Why does a lesion in the pons cause crossed hemiplegia? Because it affects descending corticospinal fibers (UMN signs contralaterally) and cranial nerve nuclei (LMN signs ipsilaterally), leading to crossed deficits. Why is the rubrospinal tract important in patients with pyramidal tract lesions? It provides an alternative pathway (corticorubrospinal route) for cortical motor commands, aiding partial recovery of fine motor control. 250 Why does the extrapyramidal system have both facilitatory and inhibitory tracts? To precisely regulate muscle tone and coordinate complex motor activities, including balance, posture, and movement suppression. Why is the extrapyramidal system considered multisynaptic? Because its pathway includes several relay nuclei (basal ganglia, thalamus, red nucleus, etc.), unlike the direct, monosynaptic pyramidal tract. Explain the mechanism by which the pyramidal tract facilitates voluntary movement. The pyramidal tract transmits impulses from motor cortex to alpha motor neurons (directly or via interneurons), initiating fine, skilled, and voluntary movement, especially in distal muscles. Lesion damages corticospinal tract (UMN) before decussation > contralateral hemiplegia, and cranial nerve nucleus at the level + ipsilateral LMN signs, resulting in crossed findings. Mechanism of sparing upper face in unilateral facial paralysis due to corticobulbar tract damage. Upper facial muscles get bilateral cortical input, so damage to one hemisphere still allows the intact hemisphere to activate the upper facial nucleus. Explain the mechanism by which uncrossed corticospinal fibers contribute to recovery. These uncrossed fibers can maintain or restore partial voluntary control over bilateral-acting muscles like respiratory or abdominal muscles, compensating for lost contralateral fibers. Faradic stimulation elicits no response; galvanic stimulation produces abnormal responses indicating reaction of degeneration. What happens to muscle tone immediately after UMNL? Initially decreased (spinal shock phase), followed by gradual development of hypertonia. Why is paralysis in UMNL usually widespread? Because lesions affect entire tracts controlling large groups of muscles rather than isolated neurons. Why is muscle wasting minimal in UMNL? Because reflex activity is intact and blood supply is maintained due to increased tone. Why can muscles recover after motor nerve injury but not after UMNL? Peripheral nerves contain neurolemma, allowing regeneration; central tracts lack neurolemma. Why are clonus and spasticity not seen in LMNL? Reflex arcs are disrupted, eliminating the basis for spasticity and clonus. Why does faradic current fail to stimulate muscles in LMNL? Chronaxie is prolonged due to degeneration, making the muscle unresponsive to rapid stimuli. Why do some muscles (like trunk muscles) recover in hemiplegia? Because it contains tightly packed descending motor fibers that are vulnerable to vascular injury. Compare in UMNL and LMNL. Cortex stimulates striatum — striatum inhibits GPi/SNr — reduced inhibition on thalamus — thalamus activates motor cortex — promotes movement. ### Q756: Enumerate the main types of non-associative learning. * Habituation * Sensitization « Short-term potentiation « Long-term potentiation Enumerate types of declarative (explicit) memory. + Semantic memory (facts) « Episodic memory (events) Enumerate mechanisms involved in the formation of long-term memory traces. * Increase in vesicle release sites + Increase in presynaptic nerve terminals + Increased neurotransmitter vesicles * Structural changes in dendritic spines Enumerate the centers involved in reflexive (implicit) memory. + Basal ganglia * Cerebellum Explain the mechanism of habituation. Habituation involves a gradual decrease in synaptic transmission due to repeated exposure to anon-harmful stimulus. This may be caused by reduced neurotransmitter release or decreased postsynaptic receptor responsiveness. 291 Explain the mechanism of classical conditioning. A conditioned stimulus (CS) is paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus (US). Over time, the CS alone elicits the same response as the US, due to associative learning and integration in the orbitofrontal cortex. Describe the mechanism of memory consolidation, Consolidation transforms short-term memory into long-term memory by repeated rehearsal and involves gene expression, new protein synthesis, and formation of permanent synaptic changes (engrams). Explain the mechanism by which working memory functions. Working memory uses prefrontal cortex circuits to temporarily hold and manipulate multiple items of information for problem-solving or planning. It relies on reverberating circuits and active neural firing. Describe the mechanism of retroactive inhibition in short-term memory. New incoming information displaces or interferes with previously stored short-term memory content, leading to forgetting of older material. Why habituation is considered a form of negative memory? Because it leads to suppression of responses to repetitive, non-significant stimuli, reducing attention to such inputs. Why is memory consolidation impaired in mentally fatigued individuals? Because effective consolidation requires repeated rehearsal and attention, both of which are diminished in mental fatigue. Why does amnesia occur following hippocampal lesions? Because the hippocampus is critical for encoding and consolidating declarative memory; damage impairs the formation of new memories (anterograde amnesia). Why can long-term memory persist even if the hippocampus is damaged later in life? Because long-term memories are stored in the neocortex, not the hippocampus, which is only essential for memory formation. Compare habituation and sensitization. What is the effect of repeatedly presenting the conditioned stimulus without the unconditioned stimulus in classical conditioning? It leads to extinction (internal inhibition), where the conditioned response gradually disappears What is the effect of applying an external distracting stimulus during a conditioned response? It can cause external inhibition, temporarily suppressing the conditioned response. What is the effect of protein synthesis inhibitors on memory? They impair long-term memory consolidation but do not affect short-term memory. What is the effect of trauma or deep anesthesia within 5 minutes of learning? It can erase short-term memory before consolidation is complete. What is the effect of pairing a previously neutral stimulus with a noxious one during learning? It causes sensitization, increasing the response to the neutral stimulus in the future. ### Q832: Enumerate the physiological changes in the circulatory system during sleep. o Decreased heart rate Decreased cardiac output (CO) Decreased vasomotor tone Decreased arterial blood pressure (ABP) Prolonged circulation time ooo 0 Enumerate the stages of non-REM sleep and their characteristic EEG patterns. o Stage 1: Light sleep, theta waves o Stage 2: Sleep spindles and K-complexes o Stage 3: Moderate deep sleep, delta waves (3-4 Hz) o Stage 4: Deepest sleep, slow delta waves (0.5-1.5 Hz) ° Enumerate the brain regions involved in sleep induction. o Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) o Nucleus of tractus solitarius o — Suprachiasmatic nucleus o Pedunculopontine and lateral dorsal tegmental nuclei (PPT and LDT) Enumerate the neurotransmitters that promote wakefulness. o Norepinephrine Serotonin ° o Acetylcholine o Histamine o Orexin (hypocretin) Enumerate the features of REM sleep. o Rapid eye movement Dreaming (remembered) Irregular HR and RR Penile erection and bruxism Marked decrease in muscle tone 2000 Explain the effect of REM sleep on respiratory and cardiovascular functions. REM sleep causes irregular heart rate and respiratory rate (usually increase) which may increase due to fluctuating autonomic activity. Explain the effect of sleep on skeletal muscle tone. Muscle tone decreases during sleep, especially during REM sleep due to active inhibition of spinal motor neurons. Explain the effect of adenosine accumulation on the sleep-wake cycle. Accumulation of adenosine in the brain after prolonged wakefulness stimulates the VLPO sleep center and inhibits arousal systems, promoting sleep. Explain the effect of sleep on renal function. Sleep increases urine formation due to decreased sympathetic tone and increased renal blood flow. Explain the effect of sleep on endocrine secretion. Most endocrine secretions decrease during sleep, except for growth hormone, which increases during non-REM sleep. Why REM sleep is called paradoxical sleep? Because the EEG during REM sleep shows rapid beta waves similar to the waking state, despite the person being deeply asleep. Why does body temperature drop during non-REM sleep? Due to a decrease in metabolic rate and reduced hypothalamic thermoregulation during non- REM sleep Why is sleep important for neuronal balance? Sleep restores natural balances among neuronal centers disturbed by prolonged wakefulness, helping maintain homeostasis. 307 Why does sleep duration decrease with age? Due to reduced sleep drive, altered circadian rhythms, and diminished secretion of sleep- promoting factors in the elderly. Why dreams are better remembered in REM sleep? Because REM sleep involves active cortical function and memory processing, making dream recall more likely. Explain the mechanism of sleep induction via the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO). VLPO neurons release GABA, which inhibits arousal systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus (e.g., orexin, monoamines), promoting sleep. Explain the mechanism of wakefulness maintenance. Wakefulness is maintained by ARAS activation, with inputs from orexinergic neurons and neurotransmitters like norepinephrine, serotonin, and acetylcholine. Explain the mechanism of REM sleep generation. REM sleep is generated by cholinergic neuron activation in the pons (PPT and LDT), which stimulate thalamocortical circuits while norepinephrine and serotonin are suppressed. Explain the mechanism by which adenosine promotes sleep. Adenosine accumulates in the brain during wakefulness, activating VLPO neurons and inhibiting arousal systems, leading to sleep onset. Explain the mechanism of sleep/wake cycle synchronization, The suprachiasmatic nucleus synchronizes circadian rhythms with light-dark cues and modulates VLPO and arousal centers to regulate sleep-wake cycles. ### Q861: Explain the effect of SCC stimulation on muscle tone post-rotation. Stimulation of SCCs causes increased muscle tone on the ipsilateral side and decreased tone on the contralateral side, helping maintain posture and balance via vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts. Explain the effect of rapid head rotation on the eyes. Rapid head rotation causes vestibulo-ocular reflex leading to nystagmus, characterized by a slow eye movement opposite to rotation and a fast correctional movement in the same direction. Explain the effect of Meniere's syndrome on vestibular function. Increased endolymph pressure in SCCs causes 312 distorted stimulation leading to vertigo, nystagmus, and vomiting, due to overstimulation of vestibular pathways. Explain the effect of stopping rotation on perception. After stopping rotation, the endolymph continues moving, causing cupula deflection in the opposite direction, leading to vertigo and post-rotatory nystagmus, Explain the effect of excessive streptomycin on vestibular function. Excess streptomycin damages the hair cells of SCCs, leading to abnormal stimulation or destruction of vestibular input, causing vertigo and imbalance. Why does nystagmus occur only at the start and end of rotation? Nystagmus results from deflection of the cupula by endolymph movement. Once endolymph and cupula move synchronously during steady rotation, no relative deflection occurs, so signals stop until rotation ceases. Why does vertigo occur after rotation stops? The momentum of endolymph causes continued movement, deflecting the cupula in the opposite direction, leading to false perception of counter rotation. Why does alcohol toxicity lead to vertigo even in static head position? Alcohol alters endolymph density, causing buoyancy-induced cupula deflection, mimicking rotation and resulting in vertigo without actual movement. Explain the mechanism of nystagmus induction during rotation. Rotation causes endolymph movement > cupula deflection in cristae — stimulation of vestibular nerve — vestibular nuclei + medial longitudinal fasciculus — activation of CN III, IV, VI > produces slow eye movement CNS QUESTIONS opposite to rotation, followed by brainstem- induced fast movement in same direction. Explain the mechanism of vertigo after rotation stops. When rotation stops, inertia causes continued endolymph flow — deflects cupula in the direction of original rotation — false signal of continued motion — brain interprets as opposite direction rotation, causing vertigo. Enumerate the functions of the vestibulo- ocular reflex (VOR). 1. Stabilizes images on the retina during head movement 2. Produces compensatory eye movement opposite to head movement Maintains clear vision during head tremors 4. Functions in total darkness or with closed eyes Enumerate the structures that receive vestibular signals. 1. Spinal cord (via vestibulospinal tracts) 2. Reticular formation 3. Cranial nerve nuclei (III, IV, VI via medial longitudinal bundle) 4. Cerebellum (vestibulocerebellum) 5. Cerebral cortex (via vestibulo-thalamo- cortical pathways) Enumerate the types of acceleration detected by components of the vestibular system. 1. Linear acceleration — detected by otolith organs (utricle and saccule) 2. Angular acceleration — detected by semicircular canals Explain the effect of head tilting on macular discharge. Head tilting causes gravity to pull the otoliths, bending the hair cell cilia, resulting in an increase or decrease in discharge depending on the direction of tilt. This altered discharge is interpreted by the CNS to determine the head position and trigger postural reflexes. 313 Describe the effect of linear acceleration on the utricle. Horizontal acceleration (e.g., bus movement) causes otoliths to lag behind due to inertia, bending cilia and stimulating hair cells, resulting in a sensation of falling backward and a reflexive forward lean. What is the effect of bending stereocilia toward the kinocilium in the crista ampullaris? Depolarization of hair cells occurs, leading to increased discharge in the vestibular nerve and excitation of the corresponding reflex pathways. What happens when the vestibulo-ocular reflex is impaired? Patients experience difficulty stabilizing their visual field during head movements, especially during activities like reading, due to inability to produce compensatory eye movements. Why does the VOR function even in total darkness? Because it is a reflex driven by vestibular input, not visual input. The semicircular canals detect head rotation and drive compensatory eye movements independent of vision. Why are SCCs insensitive to constant velocity rotation? Because once endolymph catches up to the head's rotational speed, no relative motion or cupula deflection occurs, so the cristae no longer sense movement. Describe the mechanism of detection of head tilting by the otolith organs. Gravity causes otoliths to shift — cilia bend > hair cells depolarize or hyperpolarize — pattern of discharge in vestibular nerve changes + CNS interprets direction and initiates postural reflexes. Explain the mechanism of stimulation of the cristae ampullaris during angular rotation. Head rotates + endolymph lags due to inertia — cupula bends — stereocilia bend toward or away from kinocilium — depolarization or hyperpolarization — changes in nerve impulse frequency. 314 Postural and equilibrium reflexes Compare utricle and saccule in terms of orientation and function. [ Feature Utricle Saccule F Orientation _| Horizontal plane Vertical plane Function Detect forward-backward tilt | Detect side-to-side tilt Acceleration | Horizontal Vertical Compare macula and crista ampullaris. Feature Macula Crista Ampullaris Location Uncle & Saccule Ampulla of SCCs Type of acceleration | Linear (gravity, tilting) Angular (rotational Structure Otolithic membrane with otoconia | Cupula (no otoconia) Match each component with its primary function:
- **A)** 3 B=
- **B)** Saccule 2. Detects angular acceleration
- **C)** Horizontal SCC 3. Detects linear horizontal acceleration
- **D)** Crista ampullaris 4. Mechanoreceptor in SCCs
- **E)** Macula 5. Mechanoreceptor in otolith organs

**Correct Answer:** A
**Type:** QCS
**Tag:** `Department, Physiology 2026`

### Q1056: Why are fatty acids not used as a primary energy source by the human brain?
**Model Answer:** 1. Fatty acids bound to albumin cross the blood-brain barrier very slowly. 2. Mitochondrial beta-oxidation in neurons requires high oxygen consumption, risking hypoxia and generating excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS). 3. Neurons have low levels of key beta-oxidation enzymes
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Biochemistry 2026`

### Q1057: What are the main roles of lipids in the brain?

**Tag:** `Department, Biochemistry 2026`

**Correct Answer:** -

### Q1059: Why does the human brain consume approximately 20% of resting whole-body energy?
**Model Answer:** The brain requires continuous ATP to: 1. Maintain ionic gradients across neuronal membranes via Na+/K+-ATPase pumps. 2. Drive neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicular packaging, and synaptic transmission. 3. Support axonal transport, membrane remodeling, and cellular biosynthesis
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Biochemistry 2026`

### Q1060: Explain the cerebral metabolic adaptations during feeding versus fasting states
**Model Answer:** Feeding State: Brain relies entirely on glucose; insulin promotes glycolysis and lipid synthesis. Fasting/Starvation State: Liver glycogen is depleted; liver converts fatty acids to ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate), which the brain oxidizes to acetyl-CoA to spare muscle protein from gluconeogenesis
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC

### Q1068: Explain the light microscopic (LM) and electron microscopic (EM) features of the neuronal Perikaryon
**Model Answer:** 1. Light Microscopy (LM): - Size: Ranges from 4 to 140 micrometers. - Nucleus: Large, central, spherical, euchromatic (pale-staining) with a prominent dark nucleolus ("owl-eye" appearance). - Cytoplasm: Strongly basophilic due to abundant Nissl bodies (granules) stained with basic dyes like toluidine blue; contains neurofibrils extending into axon and dendrites. 2. Electron Microscopy (EM): - Organelles: Prominent perinuclear Golgi complex, abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes (Nissl bodies), numerous mitochondria, lysosomes, and centrosome. - Cytoskeleton: Dense network of neurofilaments (intermediate filaments, 10 nm) forming the internal skeleton, and neurotubules (microtubules, 25 nm) mediating anterograde and retrograde axonal transport

### Q1070: Classify neurons according to the number of processes with histological examples
**Model Answer:** 1. Unipolar / Pseudounipolar Neurons: - Possess a single process that emerges from the soma and bifurcates like a "T" into a peripheral sensory process and a central axon entering the CNS. - Examples: Primary sensory neurons in the Dorsal Root Ganglia (DRG) of spinal nerves and sensory cranial nerve ganglia (CN V, VII, IX, X). 2. Bipolar Neurons: - Possess two distinct processes arising from opposite soma poles: one dendrite and one axon. - Examples: Bipolar cells of the retina, olfactory receptor neurons in olfactory epithelium, and spiral/vestibular ganglia of CN VIII. 3. Multipolar Neurons: - Possess one single axon and multiple branching dendrites; the most common neuron type in the nervous system. - Examples: Pyramidal cells of cerebral cortex, Purkinje cells of cerebellar cortex, and anterior horn somatic motor neurons of the spinal cord. 4. Anaxonic Neurons: - Small neurons where axons cannot be distinguished from dendrites. - Examples: Amacrine cells of the retina
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Histology 2026`

### Q1071: Differentiate histologically between Spinal Ganglia and Autonomic Ganglia
**Model Answer:** 1. Capsule: Spinal ganglia have a thick, well-defined connective tissue capsule; Autonomic ganglia have a thin, delicate capsule. 2. Arrangement of Neuronal Cell Bodies: In spinal ganglia, neurons are arranged in compact groups/clusters at the periphery separated by bundles of nerve fibers; In autonomic ganglia, neurons are randomly scattered throughout the ganglion. 3. Neuron Type: Spinal ganglia contain pseudounipolar sensory neurons with central spherical nuclei; Autonomic ganglia contain multipolar motor neurons with eccentric nuclei. 4. Satellite Glial Cells: In spinal ganglia, satellite cells form a complete, continuous ring surrounding each neuron soma; In autonomic ganglia, satellite cells form an incomplete, irregular layer. 5. Nerve Fibers: Spinal ganglia contain mostly thick, heavily myelinated sensory fibers; Autonomic ganglia contain thin preganglionic myelinated and postganglionic unmyelinated fibers

### Q1072: Differentiate between Myelination in the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) and Central Nervous System (CNS
**Model Answer:** 1. Myelin-forming Cell: PNS myelination is performed by Schwann cells (neurolemmocytes derived from neural crest); CNS myelination is performed by Oligodendrocytes (derived from neural tube neuroectoderm). 2. Extent of Myelination: One Schwann cell myelinates only a single internodal segment of a single axon; One oligodendrocyte extends multiple cytoplasmic processes to simultaneously myelinate internodes of up to 40-50 different axons. 3. Neurilemma (Sheath of Schwann): Present in PNS as the outer nucleated rim of Schwann cell cytoplasm and plasma membrane; Completely absent in CNS (oligodendrocyte cell bodies remain separate from myelin wraps). 4. Basal Lamina: Present around each Schwann cell internode in PNS; Absent in CNS myelin. 5. Protein Composition: PNS myelin contains Protein Zero (P0), PMP-22, and MBP; CNS myelin contains Proteolipid Protein (PLP), MBP, and MOG. 6. Regenerative Capacity: PNS allows robust axonal regeneration guided by proliferating Schwann cells and bands of Büngner; CNS regeneration is arrested by inhibitory glial scars (astrogliosis and Nogo-A
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q1073: Write short notes on the histological types and functions of Astrocytes
**Model Answer:** 1. Morphological Types: - Protoplasmic Astrocytes: Predominantly located in gray matter; characterized by abundant cytoplasm, a large euchromatic nucleus, and numerous short, thick, highly branched cytoplasmic processes. - Fibrous Astrocytes: Predominantly located in white matter; characterized by long, thin, straight, relatively unbranched cytoplasmic processes containing abundant glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) intermediate filaments. 2. Microscopic Features: - Cytoplasmic processes expand into vascular pedicles (perivascular end-feet) that envelope capillary basement membranes and the inner surface of the pia mater (glia limitans). 3. Key Functions: - Structural and metabolic support to neurons. - Induction and maintenance of the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB). - Uptake and recycling of excess extracellular potassium (K+ spatial buffering) and neurotransmitters (glutamate, GABA). - Repair and glial scar formation (gliosis/astrogliosis) following CNS injury
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q1074: Differentiate histologically between Microglia and Oligodendrocytes
**Model Answer:** 1. Embryological Origin: Microglia originate from mesoderm / yolk-sac hematopoietic progenitors (mononuclear phagocyte system); Oligodendrocytes originate from neuroectoderm (neural tube). 2. Location: Microglia are evenly distributed throughout both gray and white matter; Oligodendrocytes are found in white matter (interfascicular) and gray matter (perineuronal satellite cells). 3. Morphology: - Microglia: Smallest glial cells, dark elongated/spindle-shaped nuclei, and delicate wavy spiny branching processes in the resting state; transform into large, motile, amoeboid phagocytic macrophages (gitter cells) upon activation. - Oligodendrocytes: Small round cells with compact, darkly stained round nuclei and a clear cytoplasmic halo ("fried-egg" appearance on paraffin sections); possess a few short slender processes. 4. Primary Function: - Microglia: Antigen presentation, immune defense, cytokine secretion, and phagocytosis of cellular debris. - Oligodendrocytes: Synthesis and maintenance of myelin sheaths around CNS axons

### Q1075: Differentiate between non-encapsulated and encapsulated sensory nerve endings with examples
**Model Answer:** 1. ### Q1076: Explain the histological structure of the neuromuscular muscle spindle and its role in proprioception
**Model Answer:** 1. Capsule: Fusiform (spindle-shaped) multilayered connective tissue capsule enclosing a fluid-filled periaxial lymph space. 2. Intrafusal Muscle Fibers (6 to 14 fibers per spindle): - Nuclear Bag Fibers (1-2 per spindle): Dynamic and static types; central expanded bag containing a cluster of numerous nuclei; insensitive to static stretch, highly sensitive to rate of stretch. - Nuclear Chain Fibers (4-5 per spindle): Thinner, shorter fibers with nuclei arranged in a single longitudinal row; sensitive to sustained static stretch. 3. Sensory Innervation: - Primary (Ia) Afferents: Large myelinated fibers that terminate as annulospiral endings coiled around the equatorial regions of both bag and chain fibers (respond to onset and velocity of stretch). - Secondary (II) Afferents: Smaller fibers terminating as "flower-spray" endings on either side of the equator mainly on chain fibers (respond to steady-state length). 4. Motor Innervation: - Gamma motor neurons from spinal anterior horn innervate the striated contractile polar ends of intrafusal fibers, regulating receptor sensitivity and tone. 5. Proprioceptive Role: Detects changes in muscle length (stretch) and the velocity of length change, mediating the monosynaptic stretch reflex and maintaining muscle tone and posture
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC

Location: Pacinian corpuscles are located deep in the dermis, hypodermis, periosteum, joint capsules, and mesentery; Meissner's corpuscles are located superficially in dermal papillae of hairless (glabrous) skin (fingertips, palms, soles, lips). 3. ### Q1078: Write short notes on Ruffini endings and Krause end-bulbs
**Model Answer:** 1. Ruffini Endings (Corpuscles of Ruffini): - Structure: Elongated, spindle-shaped encapsulated receptors containing branched sensory nerve terminals intertwined among bundles of collagen fibers within a thin capsule. - Location: Deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, joint capsules, and periodontal ligament. - Function: Slowly adapting type II mechanoreceptors sensitive to sustained mechanical pressure, skin stretch, and joint torque/rotation. 2. Pia Mater (Leptomeninx): - Highly vascular, delicate layer of connective tissue cells and collagen fibrils tightly adherent to the outer contour of brain and spinal cord surface, following all sulci and gyri. - Separated from neural tissue by the glial limiting membrane (astrocyte end-feet

### Q1081: Explain the Rexed laminae architecture of the spinal cord gray matter
**Model Answer:** The gray matter is organized cytoarchitecturally into 10 Rexed laminae: 1. Lamina I (Posteromarginal nucleus): Caps the apex of posterior horn, receives A-delta nociceptive inputs. 2. Lamina II (Substantia Gelatinosa of Rolando): Gelatinous zone of small interneurons that modulates and gates pain/temperature transmission (Gate Control Theory). 3. Laminae III & IV (Nucleus Proprius): Main receptive zone for tactile, crude touch, and proprioceptive fibers, origin of spinothalamic tracts. 4. Lamina V & VI: Base of posterior horn; receive sensory and descending corticospinal inputs; contains Clarke's column (nucleus dorsalis, C8-L3) at base mediating dorsal spinocerebellar tract. 5. Lamina VII (Zona Intermedia): Intermediolateral sympathetic column (T1-L2) and sacral parasympathetic (S2-S4) preganglionic neurons. 6. Lamina VIII: Interneurons in anterior horn mediating reflex coordination. 7. Lamina IX: Clusters of large alpha motor neurons and gamma motor neurons innervating skeletal muscles. 8. Lamina X: Neuroglia and decussating unmyelinated axons surrounding the central canal
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC

### Q1083: Describe the ascending sensory tracts of the spinal cord and their modalities
**Model Answer:** 1. Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscal System (Fasciculus Gracilis & Fasciculus Cuneatus): - Modalities: Fine discriminative touch, conscious proprioception, two-point discrimination, and vibration sense. - Course: Ascends uncrossed in dorsal funiculus to gracile and cuneate nuclei of medulla. 2. Lateral Spinothalamic Tract: - Modalities: Pain and thermal sensations. - Course: Second-order fibers from posterior horn decussate in anterior white commissure and ascend in lateral funiculus to VPL thalamus. 3. Anterior (Ventral) Spinothalamic Tract: - Modalities: Crude (light) touch and pressure. - Course: Decussates obliquely in anterior white commissure and ascends in anterior funiculus to VPL thalamus. 4. Spinocerebellar Tracts (Dorsal and Ventral): - Modalities: Unconscious proprioception from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors to the cerebellar cortex
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q1085: Explain the nuclei and fiber tracts of the auditory pathway in the pons
**Model Answer:** 1. Cochlear Nuclei: Located at the pontomedullary junction on the lateral aspect of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei receiving primary auditory fibers of CN VIII). 2. Trapezoid Body (Corpus Trapezoideum): Prominent transverse acoustic fiber decussation in the ventral tegmentum of the caudal pons formed by crossing fibers of the ventral cochlear nuclei. 3. Superior Olivary Complex: Nuclei embedded within the trapezoid body that receive bilateral auditory input, essential for auditory localization of sound in the horizontal plane. 4. Nucleus of Trapezoid Body: Relay and inhibitory interneurons within the auditory pathway. 5. Lateral Lemniscus: Prominent ascending tract formed by crossed and uncrossed acoustic fibers originating from the trapezoid body and superior olive, coursing through the lateral pontine tegmentum to terminate in the inferior colliculus of the midbrain

### Q1086: Describe the histological levels of the pons in transverse section (caudal vs. rostral
**Model Answer:** 1. Caudal Pontine Level (Facial Colliculus Level): - Tegmentum contains the Abducent nucleus (CN VI) in the ventricular floor, encircled by motor fibers of the Facial nerve (CN VII) forming the internal genu (facial colliculus). - Motor nucleus of facial nerve located ventrolaterally. - Trapezoid body and spinal tract/nucleus of CN V present laterally. 3. Rostral Pontine Level (Trigeminal Level): - Characterized by the emergence of the large sensory and small motor nuclei of the Trigeminal nerve (CN V) in the lateral tegmentum. - Superior cerebellar peduncles (brachia conjunctiva) form the dorsolateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle, interconnected by the superior medullary velum. - Medial lemniscus rotates into a horizontal ribbon at the boundary between basilar pons and tegmentum

### Q1088: Describe the four brainstem lemnisci: origin, course, termination, and modalities
**Model Answer:** 1. ### Q1089: Enumerate and describe the histological layers of the Cerebral Cortex
**Model Answer:** The neocortex (isocortex) consists of six distinct histological laminae from superficial to deep: 1. Layer I - Molecular (Plexiform) Layer: Acellular appearance, consists mostly of horizontally oriented dendrites and axons, with few scattered horizontal cells of Cajal. 2. Layer II - External Granular Layer: Densely packed with small pyramidal cells and stellate (granule) interneurons; establishes intracortical connections. 3. Layer III - External Pyramidal Layer: Composed of medium-sized pyramidal cells whose axons form association and commissural fibers (e.g., corpus callosum). 4. Layer IV - Internal Granular Layer: Densely packed stellate cells receiving the primary specific thalamocortical afferent projections; highly developed in primary sensory cortices (granular/koniocortex). 5. Layer V - Internal Pyramidal (Ganglionic) Layer: Contains large to giant pyramidal cells (Betz cells in Area 4); principal source of subcortical efferent projection fibers (corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticostriatal tracts). 6. Layer VI - Multiform (Polymorphic) Layer: Heterogeneous mixture of fusiform and Martinotti cells, projecting corticothalamic feedback fibers back to the thalamus
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Histology 2026`

### Q1090: Enumerate and describe the histological layers and synaptic circuitry of the Cerebellar Cortex
**Model Answer:** 1. Three Histological Layers (superficial to deep): - Molecular Layer: Low cellularity; contains outer stellate cells, inner basket cells, parallel fibers (unmyelinated axons of granule cells), and the extensive dendritic arbors of Purkinje cells. - Purkinje Cell Layer: Monolayer of huge, flask-shaped Purkinje neurons; their heavily branched dendritic trees receive excitatory climbing and parallel fibers; their axons provide the sole inhibitory (GABAergic) outflow from cerebellar cortex to deep cerebellar nuclei. - Granular Layer: Extremely cellular; contains millions of tightly packed tiny granule cells (glutamatergic excitatory interneurons) and inhibitory Golgi type II cells, forming complex synaptic complexes called cerebellar glomeruli. 2. Afferent Input Fibers: - Climbing Fibers: Originate exclusively from contralateral inferior olivary nucleus, wrap directly around Purkinje dendrites, firing powerful "complex spikes". - Mossy Fibers: Originate from all other sources (vestibular, spinocerebellar, pontocerebellar), terminate in cerebellar glomeruli on granule cell dendrites, firing "simple spikes
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q1091: Describe the histological structure and function of the Choroid Plexus
**Model Answer:** 1. Location: Folds of vascular tela choroidea projecting into the lateral, third, and fourth brain ventricles. 2. Histological Structure: - Core: Highly vascularized, loose connective tissue stroma derived from pia mater, containing wide, fenestrated capillaries (allowing rapid fluid exchange). - Epithelial Lining: Single continuous layer of specialized modified cuboidal ependymal cells (choroid epithelial cells) resting on a basement membrane. - Apical Surface: Expanded with prominent microvilli forming a brush border that increases surface area for secretion. - Intercellular Junctions: Sealed apicolaterally by continuous, impermeable tight junctions (zonulae occludentes), which constitute the functional Blood-CSF Barrier. 3. Function: Active secretion of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via energy-dependent ion transport (Na+/K+ ATPase pumps, carbonic anhydrase, and aquaporin-1 water channels); secretes ~500 mL of CSF daily

### Q1092: Enumerate and describe the histological components of the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB
**Model Answer:** The Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) is a highly selective physiological boundary composed of three essential morphological elements: 1. Non-fenestrated Capillary Endothelium: - Continuous capillary endothelial cells lacking transcellular fenestrations or pinocytotic vesicles. - Joined together by continuous, high-resistance, impermeable tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) composed of transmembrane proteins (claudin-3, claudin-5, occludin) linked to the cytoskeleton via zonula occludens (ZO-1, ZO-2) scaffolding proteins. 2. Continuous Capillary Basal Lamina: - Thick, uninterrupted basement membrane enveloping the abluminal endothelial surface and embedding pericytes. 3. Perivascular Astrocytic End-Feet (Podocytes): - Foot processes of protoplasmic and fibrous astrocytes that almost completely (approx. 95%) encircle and sheath the outer capillary wall, inducing and maintaining endothelial tight junction integrity through biochemical signaling (e.g., sonic hedgehog, angiopoietin-1). (Pericytes also reside within the basal lamina, regulating capillary diameter and endothelial stability

### Q1093: Enumerate and describe the histological components of the Blood-CSF Barrier and contrast it with the Blood-Brain Barrier
**Model Answer:** 1. Blood-CSF Barrier Components (in Choroid Plexus): - Fenestrated capillary endothelium: Capillaries inside choroid plexus are fenestrated and permeable to water and solutes. - Pial connective tissue stroma: Intervening loose basement membrane and connective tissue. - Choroid Plexus Epithelial Cells: Simple cuboidal ependymal cells joined apically by continuous, impermeable tight junctions (zonulae occludentes). The barrier is therefore located at the choroid epithelial cell layer, NOT at the capillary endothelium. 2. Contrast with Blood-Brain Barrier: - Site of Tight Junctions: In the BBB, tight junctions are located between capillary endothelial cells; in the Blood-CSF barrier, tight junctions are located between epithelial ependymal cells of the choroid plexus. - Capillary Type: BBB capillaries are continuous and non-fenestrated; Choroid plexus capillaries are fenestrated. - Astrocyte End-Feet: Essential for BBB formation; absent at the choroid plexus
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Histology 2026`

### Q1098: Compare between Sabin (OPV) and Salk (IPV) Poliovirus vaccines
**Model Answer:** Sabin (OPV): - Type: Live attenuated virus (oral drops). - Immunity: Induces both systemic IgG and mucosal secretory IgA in gut (prevents viral shedding and provides herd immunity). - Administration: Oral, easy, inexpensive. - Disadvantages: Risk of Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) and circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV); contraindicated in immunodeficiency. Salk (IPV): - Type: Formalin-inactivated virus (intramuscular injection). - Immunity: Induces strong humoral IgG preventing CNS invasion, but minimal intestinal IgA (does not prevent reinfection or fecal shedding). - Administration: Injection, requires cold chain and trained staff. - Safety: Safe in immunocompromised individuals; zero risk of VAPP
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Microbiology 2026`

### Q1099: Compare between the clinical features and mechanisms of Tetanus and Botulism
**Model Answer:** Tetanus (Clostridium tetani): - Toxin: Tetanospasmin. - Mechanism: Retrograde axonal transport to CNS Renshaw inhibitory interneurons, cleaving synaptobrevin and blocking release of inhibitory transmitters (Glycine and GABA). - Clinical effect: Unopposed motor excitation causing spastic spasticity, trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, and opisthotonos. Botulism (Clostridium botulinum): - Toxin: Botulinum neurotoxin (7 serotypes A-G). - Mechanism: Acts peripherally at the neuromuscular junction, cleaving SNARE proteins to block acetylcholine release. - Clinical effect: Symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis, starting with cranial nerves (diplopia, dysphagia, ptosis), fixed dilated pupils, and respiratory failure without sensory loss
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Microbiology 2026`

### Q1103: Describe the transmission and pathogenesis of Rabies virus in humans
**Model Answer:** Transmission: Inoculation of infected saliva via bite, scratch, or lick on broken skin/mucosa from rabid mammals (dogs, wolves, bats). Pathogenesis: Virus replicates locally in striated muscle cells -> enters peripheral unmyelinated nerve endings via nicotinic acetylcholine receptors -> travels by retrograde fast axonal transport (50-100 mm/day) along sensory/motor axons to dorsal root ganglia and spinal cord -> spreads rapidly throughout brain causing acute encephalomyelitis with predilection for limbic system and hippocampus (forming cytoplasmic Negri bodies) -> centripetal centrifugal spread via nerves to salivary glands, cornea, and skin
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Microbiology 2026`

### Q1129: Outline the comprehensive management protocol for a confirmed case of Clostridium tetani infection
**Model Answer:** 1. Passive immunotherapy: Immediate intramuscular administration of Human Tetanus Immune Globulin (HTIG, 3000-6000 units) to neutralize circulating unbound tetanospasmin. 2. Wound debridement: Surgical cleansing, debridement of necrotic tissue, and removal of foreign bodies to eradicate anaerobic focus. 3. Antibiotic therapy: Metronidazole (preferred) or Penicillin G to eliminate vegetative bacilli. 4. Supportive airway and muscle spasm control: Mechanical ventilation, dark and quiet isolation room, intravenous benzodiazepines (diazepam) and neuromuscular blockers. 5. Active immunization: Tetanus toxoid vaccine given at a different site (clinical disease does not confer immunity
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q1177: Compare between Acute and Chronic Opioid Toxicity in terms of causes, clinical picture, and management
**Model Answer:** Acute Opioid Toxicity: - Cause: Administration of large single overdose. - Clinical picture (Classic triad): Coma, pinpoint pupils (miosis), and severe respiratory depression (shallow, slow breathing, cyanosis). - Management: Airway protection and mechanical ventilation, gastric lavage (if ingested), and specific antidote Naloxone IV (0.4-2 mg repeated as needed). Chronic Opioid Toxicity (Dependence/Tolerance): - Cause: Repeated long-term administration. - Clinical picture: High tolerance to analgesia/euphoria (no tolerance to miosis or constipation); physical and psychological dependence; severe withdrawal syndrome (rhinorrhea, lacrimation, yawning, piloerection, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, tremors) upon discontinuation. - Management: Gradual detoxification with long-acting opioids (Methadone or Buprenorphine), psychological support, and Clonidine for autonomic symptoms
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Pharmacology 2026`

### Q1194: Describe the mechanism of action, side effects, and contraindications of Ergot alkaloids in migraine
**Model Answer:** Mechanism of action: Non-selective partial agonists at 5-HT1B/1D serotonin, alpha-adrenergic, and dopamine receptors. Induce vasoconstriction of dilated intracranial blood vessels and decrease release of vasodilator neuropeptides from trigeminal nerve endings. Side effects: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, anginal chest pain, peripheral ischemia/paresthesia (ergotism), and rebound medication-overuse headache upon prolonged use. Contraindications: Pregnancy (oxytocic action causing uterine contractions), peripheral vascular disease, ischemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, renal/hepatic impairment, and co-administration with triptans
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC

### Q1195: Describe the mechanism of action, side effects, and contraindications of Triptans in migraine
**Model Answer:** Mechanism of action: Selective agonists at 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors: 1. 5-HT1B stimulation causes selective vasoconstriction of painful dilated intracranial and dural vessels. 2. 5-HT1D presynaptic stimulation inhibits release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P from trigeminal sensory afferents. 3. Inhibits central transmission in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis. Side effects: Tingling, warmth, burning sensation, dizziness, neck and chest tightness ("triptan chest sensations"), coronary vasospasm. Contraindications (HIRP): History of ischemic heart disease / angina / prior MI, uncontrolled hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease / prior stroke or TIA, severe hepatic/renal impairment, and concurrent use with MAOIs, SSRIs, or ergotamines within 24 hours
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Pharmacology 2026`

### Q1226: Describe the clinical features and management of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS
**Model Answer:** Clinical features: Hyperthermia (severe fever), severe "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, autonomic instability (fluctuating blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis), and altered mental status (delirium, stupor, coma). Pharmacological therapy: Dantrolene (skeletal muscle relaxant inhibiting calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum), Bromocriptine or Amantadine (dopamine agonists to overcome D2 blockade), and Diazepam for muscle spasms

### Q1227: Explain why Antidepressant drugs typically show clinical therapeutic effects only after 2 to 3 weeks of continuous treatment
**Model Answer:** Although neurotransmitter reuptake inhibition occurs immediately, initial increased synaptic monoamines stimulate presynaptic inhibitory autoreceptors (5-HT1A, alpha-2), which downregulates neuronal firing. Over 2 to 3 weeks of continuous therapy, these presynaptic autoreceptors become desensitized and downregulated, allowing sustained increase in postsynaptic monoaminergic neurotransmission, upregulation of secondary messenger cascades (cAMP, CREB), and induction of Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) promoting neuronal plasticity
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Pharmacology 2026`

**Model Answer:** Mechanism of action: Inhibit presynaptic neuronal reuptake pumps for both serotonin (5-HT) and noradrenaline (NE), increasing their concentration in synaptic clefts. Uses: 1. Major depressive disorder. 2. Nocturnal enuresis in children (imipramine). 3. Premature ejaculation. 4. Chronic neuropathic pain syndromes and migraine prophylaxis (amitriptyline). Side effects (Mnemonic TCAS): Tachycardia and cardiac arrhythmias (quinidine-like cardiotoxicity), anticholinergic atropine-like effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention), Sedation and orthostatic hypotension (alpha-1 blockade), Sexual dysfunction. **Correct Answer:** -

### Q1236: Describe the mechanism of action and clinical uses of Benzodiazepines (BZDs
**Model Answer:** Mechanism of action: Bind allosterically to specific benzodiazepine (BZ) receptor sites on the GABA-A receptor complex, increasing the frequency of chloride (Cl-) channel opening in response to GABA. This increases Cl- influx, causing neuronal membrane hyperpolarization and reduced neuronal excitability (positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A). Uses: 1. Generalized anxiety and panic disorders. 2. Insomnia (short-term). 3. Status epilepticus and acute seizures. 4. Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (prevents delirium tremens). 5. Preanesthetic medication and conscious procedural sedation
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Pharmacology 2026`

Uses: Reversal of benzodiazepine sedation after procedural anesthesia; diagnosis and treatment of acute benzodiazepine overdose. Adverse effects: Nausea, projectile vomiting, precipitation of acute severe benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome (agitation, tachycardia), and seizures (especially in patients with underlying epilepsy or TCA co-ingestion

### Q1239: Describe the mechanism of action of Barbiturates and contrast it with Benzodiazepines
**Model Answer:** Barbiturates bind to distinct sites on the GABA-A receptor complex and increase the duration of chloride channel opening (whereas Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of opening). At higher concentrations, barbiturates can directly open chloride channels even in the absence of GABA (GABA-mimetic action) and depress excitatory AMPA glutamate receptors, resulting in a much lower margin of safety and higher risk of fatal respiratory arrest
**Correct Answer:** -

It does not interact with GABA receptors

### Q1243: Describe the mechanism of action of Local Anesthetics
**Model Answer:** Uncharged local anesthetic molecules diffuse across the lipid neuronal membrane into the axoplasm, where they become protonated (ionized) and bind reversibly to specific receptor sites inside the voltage-gated sodium channels. This blocks sodium influx, prevents membrane depolarization, and arrests the generation and conduction of action potentials along the nerve axon

### Q1244: Compare between Ester-linked and Amide-linked Local Anesthetics
**Model Answer:** Ester-linked (e.g. Cocaine, Procaine, Tetracaine): - Duration: Short duration of action. - Metabolism: Rapidly hydrolyzed in plasma by pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase). - Allergic potential: Higher allergy risk due to formation of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite. - Stability: Less stable in solution. Amide-linked (e.g. Lidocaine, Bupivacaine, Prilocaine): - Duration: Longer duration of action. - Metabolism: Degraded by hepatic microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes. - Allergic potential: Very low allergy risk (rare cross-reactivity). - Stability: Highly stable

### Q1251: Enumerate the standard classes of Preanesthetic medications and explain the therapeutic purpose of each
**Model Answer:** 1. Sedatives / Anxiolytics (Benzodiazepines: e.g. Midazolam): - Relieve preoperative anxiety, provide sedation, reduce CNS toxicity risk, and produce anterograde amnesia. 2. Opioids (e.g. Fentanyl, Morphine): - Decrease apprehension, provide preemptive analgesia, reduce the required dose of general anesthetics, and ensure smooth induction. 3. Anticholinergic drugs (e.g. Atropine, Glycopyrrolate): - Reduce excessive salivary, pharyngeal, and bronchial secretions, and prevent reflex vagal bradycardia and hypotension. 4. H2-receptor antagonists and Proton Pump Inhibitors (e.g. Ranitidine, Omeprazole): - Reduce gastric acid volume and acidity to prevent chemical Mendelson aspiration pneumonitis. 5. Antiemetics (e.g. Metoclopramide, Ondansetron): - Prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), enhance gastric emptying, and increase lower esophageal sphincter tone
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Department, Pharmacology 2026`

### Q2083: Discuss filum terminale: Definition, extension, and attachments
**Model Answer:** Definition: Prolongation of pia mater extending from apex of conus medullaris downward to back of coccyx (length ~20 cm). Extension: From conus medullaris (lower border of L1 in adults) to back of first coccygeal vertebra (Co1). Parts & Attachments: 1. Filum terminale internum (upper 15 cm): Lies inside dural sac and subarachnoid space surrounded by cauda equina, extending down to S2 vertebra. 2. Filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament, lower 5 cm): Pierces dural sac at S2, acquires dura/arachnoid investment, and attaches to dorsal surface of Co1
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2021`

### Q2084: Define dural venous sinuses and mention their characteristics
**Model Answer:** Definition: Venous channels between endosteal and meningeal layers of cranial dura mater. Characteristics: 1. Devoid of muscular tissue in walls. 2. Lined by endothelium. 3. Valveless, permitting bidirectional flow depending on pressure gradients. 4. Rigidly held open by dura and cranial bones, preventing collapse when severed

### Q2088: Define Subthalamic Nucleus (body of Luys) and its clinical significance
**Model Answer:** Definition: Biconvex lens-shaped nucleus of diencephalon located ventral to thalamus, lateral to hypothalamus, and dorsal to substantia nigra. Connections & Neurotransmitter: Excitatory glutamatergic nucleus in basal ganglia indirect pathway; receives GABAergic inhibition from GPe and projects excitatory glutamate to GPi and SNr. Clinical significance: Lesion (usually lacunar stroke) causes hemiballismus (violent, uncontrollable, rapid flinging movements of contralateral extremities
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2021`

### Q2089: What are the four types of glial cells in the CNS and their main functions?
**Model Answer:** 1. Astrocytes: Protoplasmic (gray matter) and fibrous (white matter). Maintain blood-brain barrier (BBB), regulate extracellular K+ and glutamate reuptake, form glial scar (gliosis). 2. Oligodendrocytes: Myelinate multiple CNS axons, enabling fast saltatory conduction. 3. Microglia: Resident macrophages derived from mesoderm (monocytes); perform phagocytosis and immune surveillance. 4. Ependymal cells: Ciliated cells lining brain ventricles and spinal central canal; participate in CSF circulation and form choroid plexus epithelium
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2021`

### Q2090: Enumerate 3 extrapyramidal motor tracts and state their functions
**Model Answer:** 1. Rubrospinal tract: Originates in red nucleus; facilitates contralateral limb flexor tone and inhibits extensors. 2. Vestibulospinal tract: Originates in lateral vestibular nucleus; facilitates ipsilateral extensor antigravity muscles to maintain balance and posture. 3. Reticulospinal tract: Pontine reticulospinal facilitates extensors; medullary reticulospinal inhibits voluntary movements and extensors
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2091: List the brainstem lemnisci, their sensory modalities, and their terminations
**Model Answer:** 1. Medial lemniscus: Conscious proprioception, fine touch, vibration from gracile/cuneate nuclei to VPL nucleus of thalamus. 2. Spinal lemniscus (spinothalamic): Pain, temperature, crude touch from contralateral dorsal horn to VPL nucleus of thalamus. 3. Trigeminal lemniscus: Sensation from face and head (trigeminal sensory nuclei) to VPM nucleus of thalamus. 4. Lateral lemniscus: Auditory pathway from cochlear nuclei and superior olive to inferior colliculus
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2092: Enumerate the microscopic layers of the cerebellar cortex and their cellular components
**Model Answer:** 1. Molecular layer (outermost): Stellate cells, basket cells, Purkinje cell dendrites, and parallel fibers of granule cells. 2. Purkinje cell layer (middle): Monolayer of large flask-shaped Purkinje cells; represents the sole inhibitory (GABAergic) output of cerebellar cortex. 3. Granular layer (innermost): Densely packed granule cells (glutamatergic) and Golgi type II cells, forming cerebellar glomeruli with mossy fibers
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2094: Demonstrate the mechanism of Babinski sign (extensor plantar response
**Model Answer:** Mechanism: - Normal flexor response: S1 stimulation causes plantar flexion of toes because corticospinal tract tonically suppresses primitive spinal withdrawal reflex. - Babinski sign: Corticospinal (pyramidal) lesion abolishes descending cortical inhibition, unmasking primitive multi-synaptic spinal flexion withdrawal reflex; lateral sole stimulation produces great toe dorsiflexion and fanning of remaining toes
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2095: Explain the effect of excessive stretch of the skeletal muscle (Inverse stretch reflex / Autogenic inhibition
**Model Answer:** Mechanism of Inverse Stretch Reflex (Golgi Tendon Reflex): Excessive contraction or stretch produces extreme tension on Golgi tendon organs (GTOs). Ib afferent fibers carry impulses to spinal cord and stimulate inhibitory interneurons. Inhibitory interneurons release glycine/GABA, inhibiting alpha motor neurons supplying contracting muscle, causing sudden relaxation (clasp-knife reaction) and preventing avulsion/tendon rupture
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2021`

### Q2110: Describe the blood-brain barrier: Structural components and physiological importance
**Model Answer:** Components: 1. Continuous non-fenestrated capillary endothelium with tight junctions (zonulae occludentes). 2. Continuous endothelial basement membrane. 3. ### Q2111: Describe the course and termination of the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract

### Q2165: Define referred pain and discuss two mechanisms explaining it
**Model Answer:** Definition: Pain perceived at a cutaneous somatic site distant from the actual deep visceral or musculoskeletal source of tissue damage. Mechanisms: 1. Convergence-Projection Theory: Visceral pain afferents and cutaneous somatic nociceptive afferents converge onto the same second-order projection neurons (spinothalamic tract) in the dorsal horn. Because the brain is accustomed to receiving signals from the skin, it misinterprets visceral input as originating from the somatic dermatome. 2. Facilitation Theory: Subthreshold visceral impulses do not directly activate spinothalamic neurons but produce a subliminal excitatory fringe, facilitating sensory input from normal somatic cutaneous receptors
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC

### Q2166: Compare between the stretch reflex and the inverse stretch reflex
**Model Answer:** 1. Receptor: Stretch = Muscle spindle (intrafusal fibers); Inverse stretch = Golgi tendon organ (in tendon series). 2. Synapse: Stretch = Monosynaptic (direct to alpha motor neuron); Inverse stretch = Disynaptic/polysynaptic (via inhibitory interneurons). 4. Effector response: Stretch = Contraction of stretched muscle; Inverse stretch = Sudden relaxation of contracting muscle (autogenic inhibition). 5. Physiological role: Stretch = Maintenance of muscle tone and posture; Inverse stretch = Protection of muscle and tendon from avulsion/tearing

### Q2168: Compare between Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) and Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) lesions
**Model Answer:** 1. Muscle paralysis: UMN = Spastic paralysis (hypertonia) involving groups of muscles; LMN = Flaccid paralysis (hypotonia/atonia) of individual muscles. 2. Muscle tone: UMN = Hypertonia (clasp-knife spasticity); LMN = Hypotonia or atonia (flaccidity). 3. Tendon reflexes: UMN = Hyperactive/exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, clonus; LMN = Depressed or completely absent reflexes (hyporeflexia/areflexia). 4. Superficial reflexes: UMN = Lost (abdominal, cremasteric); LMN = Lost if reflex arc is involved. 5. Pathological reflexes: UMN = Babinski sign present; LMN = Absent. 6. Muscle wasting: UMN = Minimal (disuse atrophy only); LMN = Severe, rapid, denervation atrophy. 7. Fasciculations: UMN = Absent; LMN = Characteristic fasciculations and fibrillations present
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2169: Compare between Sabin (OPV) and Salk (IPV) poliomyelitis vaccines
**Model Answer:** 1. Type: Sabin = Live attenuated virus; Salk = Formalin-inactivated (killed) virus. 2. Route: Sabin = Oral drops; Salk = Intramuscular or subcutaneous injection. 3. Immune response: Sabin = Induces systemic IgG and local secretory intestinal IgA (mucosal immunity); Salk = Induces systemic serum IgG only, without mucosal IgA. 4. Prevention of transmission: Sabin = Blocks gut replication and prevents shed/transmission (provides strong herd immunity); Salk = Prevents paralytic CNS disease but allows wild virus intestinal shedding. 5. Risk: Sabin = Rare reversion to neurovirulence causing vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP); Salk = Zero risk of VAPP, safe in immunocompromised
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2171: Explain why it is challenging to produce botulinum toxoid compared to tetanus toxoid
**Model Answer:** 1. Lethal Potency & Biosafety: Botulinum toxin is the most poisonous biological substance known (LD50 ~1 ng/kg), imposing stringent biosafety level 3/4 containment during mass cultivation. 2. Serotypic Diversity: Clostridium botulinum elaborates 7 antigenically distinct toxins (A through G), necessitating a polyvalent toxoid, whereas Clostridium tetani produces a single uniform neurotoxin (tetanospasmin). 3. Antigenic Inactivation: Chemical formaldehyde detoxification easily destroys the heat-labile protective neutralizing epitopes of botulinum toxin, yielding low immunogenicity, unlike the highly stable tetanus toxoid
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2172: Describe the cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease and the mechanism of levodopa therapy
**Model Answer:** Cardinal Features (TRAP): 1. Tremor: Resting pill-rolling tremor (4-6 Hz), worse at rest and damped during voluntary movement. 2. Rigidity: Lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity affecting flexors and extensors equally. 3. Akinesia / Bradykinesia: Slowness in initiating and executing movements, masked facies (hypomimia), reduced arm swing. 4. Postural instability: Stooped posture, shuffling festinating gait, and impaired postural reflexes. Mechanism of Levodopa: Levodopa is the metabolic precursor of dopamine that crosses the blood-brain barrier via the large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1). In the striatum, it is decarboxylated by L-aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (dopa decarboxylase) into dopamine within surviving dopaminergic terminals, restoring dopamine transmission in the striatum
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2173: Describe the clinical features and pharmacological management of Trigeminal Neuralgia (tic douloureux
**Model Answer:** Clinical Features: Sudden, excruciating, unilateral, brief paroxysmal lancinating / electric shock-like facial pain confined to the distribution of one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most commonly V2 or V3), triggered by light touch, chewing, shaving, or wind on trigger zones. Pharmacological Management: First-line: Carbamazepine (or Oxcarbazepine), a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker that reduces high-frequency repetitive neuronal firing. Alternative/add-on: Baclofen (GABA-B agonist), Gabapentin, or surgical microvascular decompression of aberrant cerebellar artery compressing the nerve root
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2174: Describe the production, circulation, and absorption pathways of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF
**Model Answer:** Production: Produced at ~500 mL/day primarily by choroid plexuses in lateral, third, and fourth ventricles via active ependymal secretion and capillary ultrafiltration. Circulation: Lateral ventricles -> Interventricular foramina of Monro -> Third ventricle -> Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius -> Fourth ventricle -> Foramina of Luschka (lateral) and Magendie (median) -> Subarachnoid space and basal cisterns -> Circulates upward around cerebral hemispheres and downward around spinal cord. Absorption: Filtered into dural venous sinuses (primarily superior sagittal sinus) through arachnoid villi and granulations via unidirectional hydrostatic pressure gradient
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2175: Describe the course and decussation of the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract
**Model Answer:** Origin: Betz cells and pyramidal neurons of Brodmann area 4 (30%), area 6 (30%), and primary sensory areas 3, 1, 2 (40%). Course: Corona radiata -> Posterior limb of internal capsule -> Middle 3/5 of crus cerebri in ventral midbrain -> Basilar pons (longitudinal fascicles) -> Medullary pyramids. Decussation: At lower border of medulla, 85-90% of fibers decussate in the pyramidal decussation to form the Lateral Corticospinal Tract in the lateral white column of the spinal cord; remaining 10-15% uncrossed fibers form the Anterior Corticospinal Tract, which crosses at the segmental level
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

---

### Q2176: Describe the sequence of histological events during Wallerian degeneration of a peripheral nerve
**Model Answer:** 1. Distal Axon and Myelin Disintegration: Within 24-48 hours after transection, axonal neurofilaments fragment, followed by collapse and fragmentation of the myelin sheath into ovoids and lipid droplets. 2. Phagocytosis: Schwann cells divide and along with recruited blood macrophages phagocytose axonal and myelin debris (completed within 1-2 weeks). 3. Formation of Bands of Büngner: Proliferating Schwann cells align longitudinally within intact endoneurial basal lamina tubes to form cellular conduits (Bands of Büngner) that secrete neurotrophic factors (NGF) and guide regenerating axonal sprouts (growing at 1-3 mm/day). 4. Retrograde Chromatolysis: In the cell body, eccentric nucleus migration, Nissl substance dispersion (chromatolysis), and cellular swelling reflect upregulated protein synthesis for regeneration
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2177: Compare CSF findings in Acute Bacterial, Viral (Aseptic), and Tuberculous Meningitis
**Model Answer:** 1. Pressure: Bacterial = Markedly elevated (>200-300 mm H2O); Viral = Normal to slightly elevated; Tuberculous = Markedly elevated. 2. Appearance: Bacterial = Turbid / purulent; Viral = Clear; Tuberculous = Clear or opalescent with cobweb fibrin clot. 3. Leukocytes: Bacterial = Polymorphonuclear (neutrophilic) pleocytosis (1,000-10,000/mm3); Viral = Lymphocytic pleocytosis (50-500/mm3); Tuberculous = Lymphocytic pleocytosis (100-500/mm3). 4. Protein: Bacterial = Markedly elevated (>100-500 mg/dL); Viral = Normal to mildly elevated (<100 mg/dL); Tuberculous = Markedly elevated (often >500 mg/dL). 5. Glucose: Bacterial = Markedly reduced (<40 mg/dL or CSF:serum ratio <0.4); Viral = Normal (>60% of serum glucose); Tuberculous = Markedly reduced (<30 mg/dL
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2178: Describe the course, synaptic relays, and termination of the Lateral Spinothalamic Tract
**Model Answer:** 1. First-Order Neurons: Pseudounipolar neurons in dorsal root ganglion carrying pain and temperature (A-delta and C fibers); enter spinal cord via dorsolateral tract of Lissauer and synapse on neurons in Rexed laminae I, II (substantia gelatinosa), and V of dorsal horn. 2. Second-Order Neurons: Dorsal horn projection neurons whose axons cross obliquely through the anterior white commissure to the opposite lateral white column, ascending as the lateral spinothalamic tract (spinal lemniscus) through medulla, pons, and midbrain. 3. Third-Order Neurons: Synapse in the Ventral Posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of thalamus, which projects through the posterior limb of internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2) in the postcentral gyrus
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2179: Describe the classical clinical triad of acute cerebellar hemisphere lesion
**Model Answer:** 1. Intention Tremor: Tremor that appears during visually guided voluntary goal-directed movement and intensifies as the target is approached. 2. Dysmetria: Inability to properly judge distance and scale movements, resulting in past-pointing (overshooting or undershooting a target) on finger-to-nose testing. 3. Dysdiadochokinesia: Inability to perform rapid, alternating movements smoothly (e.g., rapid pronation-supination of hands
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2180: Describe the clinical features and anatomical basis of Syringomyelia
**Model Answer:** Anatomical Basis: Cavitation / syrinx formation within the central canal of the cervical spinal cord, which progressively expands and destroys the decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure. Clinical Features: 1. Dissociated Sensory Loss: Bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations with preservation of light touch, vibration, and proprioception (dorsal columns spared). 2. Segmental 'Cape-like' Distribution: Sensory deficit spans the shoulders, upper chest, and upper extremities. 3. Lower Motor Neuron signs in upper extremities (wasting of small hand muscles) from ventral horn anterior expansion. 4. Upper Motor Neuron signs in lower extremities from late corticospinal compression
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2022`

### Q2315: Synaptic integration within a small neuronal network was studied in the laboratory. ### Q2346: Explain why lumbar puncture is safely performed below the L3 level in adults
**Model Answer:** In adults, the spinal cord (conus medullaris) terminates at the level of the lower border of L1 (or upper border of L2). Below this level, the subarachnoid space forms the wide lumbar cistern, which contains only the cauda equina nerve roots and filum terminale floating freely in CSF. Performing lumbar puncture at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 intervertebral space avoids direct needle injury to the spinal cord, as the mobile nerve roots easily slide away from the puncture needle
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2349: Describe the molecular basis of Alzheimer disease regarding protein misfolding and key pathogenic features
**Model Answer:** 1. Amyloid-Beta (Aβ42) Plaque Formation: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) normally undergoes non-amyloidogenic cleavage by alpha-secretase. In Alzheimer's disease, sequential cleavage of APP by beta-secretase (BACE1) and gamma-secretase (presenilin complex) generates insoluble, toxic amyloid-beta (Aβ42) monomers that misfold and aggregate into oligomers and extracellular senile/neuritic plaques, triggering neuroinflammation and synaptic loss. 2. Neurofibrillary Tangles (NFTs): Microtubule-associated protein tau undergoes pathological hyperphosphorylation, causing it to detach from axonal microtubules. Free hyperphosphorylated tau self-assembles into paired helical filaments, forming intracellular NFTs that disrupt axonal transport and lead to neuronal apoptosis. 3. Gross Neuropathology: Severe cortical atrophy with marked enlargement of ventricles (hydrocephalus ex vacuo), especially in hippocampus and temporoparietal cortex
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2025`

### Q2350: Discuss the physiological mechanism of presynaptic inhibition
**Model Answer:** Presynaptic inhibition is mediated at axo-axonic synapses where an inhibitory neuron terminates on the excitatory presynaptic axon terminal. The inhibitory interneuron releases GABA, which binds to GABAA receptors (increasing chloride conductance) or GABAB receptors (closing voltage-gated calcium channels). This local depolarization or hyperpolarization dampens the arriving action potential and decreases Ca2+ influx into the presynaptic terminal. Consequently, the exocytosis of excitatory neurotransmitter (e.g., glutamate) is significantly diminished, reducing the amplitude of the postsynaptic EPSP without altering the postsynaptic membrane potential directly
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2025`

### Q2351: Explain the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in the formation of long-term memory (LTP
**Model Answer:** 1. Induction of Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) in Hippocampus: High-frequency tetanic stimulation causes sustained glutamate release that strongly activates AMPA receptors, causing prolonged postsynaptic depolarization. 2. Removal of Mg2+ Block: Membrane depolarization expels the magnesium (Mg2+) ion blocking NMDA receptor channels, allowing a massive influx of calcium (Ca2+) into the dendritic spine. 3. Intracellular Cascade: Calcium activates protein kinases, primarily Calcium/Calmodulin-dependent Protein Kinase II (CaMKII) and Protein Kinase C (PKC). 4. Early Expression: Phosphorylation and rapid trafficking/insertion of additional AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane, enhancing synaptic sensitivity to glutamate. 5. Late Maintenance & Synaptic Remodeling: Ca2+ activates adenylate cyclase and PKA, activating CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) transcription factors in the nucleus, inducing gene transcription and synthesis of new structural proteins (actin, tubulin) that enlarge dendritic spines and generate new synaptic boutons
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2025`

### Q2356: Define dark adaptation and explain its physiological basis
**Model Answer:** Definition: The process by which the visual threshold of the retina declines and light sensitivity progressively increases when the eye transitions from bright light to darkness. Physiological Basis (Biphasic Curve): 1. First Phase (Cone Adaptation): Rapid, occurring during the first 5 to 10 minutes. Cones have a rapid rate of photopigment regeneration, but achieve only a modest increase in visual sensitivity (scotopic threshold remains high). 2. Second Phase (Rod Adaptation): Slower, beginning after 7-10 minutes and continuing for 30 to 45 minutes. Rods slowly regenerate rhodopsin from 11-cis-retinal and opsin, achieving a dramatic 100,000-fold increase in light sensitivity, adapting the visual system for low-light scotopic vision
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2025`

### Q2357: Why do passengers swallow or chew gum during airplane ascent and descent?
**Model Answer:** During rapid changes in altitude, atmospheric pressure in the cabin changes rapidly relative to air trapped in the middle ear cavity, producing a pressure differential across the tympanic membrane that causes ear discomfort, pain, and muffled hearing. Swallowing or chewing activates the tensor veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus muscles, which actively dilate and open the pharyngeal orifice of the auditory (Eustachian) tube, allowing air to flow between the nasopharynx and middle ear, thereby equalizing middle ear pressure with atmospheric pressure
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2358: Describe the servocomparator function of the spinocerebellum
**Model Answer:** The spinocerebellum (intermediate zone of cerebellar hemisphere and vermis) acts as a real-time 'comparator' or servocomparator to coordinate ongoing movements: 1. Receives an 'efference copy' (intended motor command) from the motor cortex via corticopontocerebellar pathways. 2. Simultaneously receives real-time sensory feedback regarding actual ongoing movement from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors via the dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts. 3. The spinocerebellum compares intended movement with actual performance. If an error or discrepancy is detected, it calculates corrective signals and transmits them via the interposed and dentate nuclei to the motor cortex (via thalamus) and red nucleus/rubrospinal tract to adjust muscle contractions and maintain smooth, coordinated execution
**Correct Answer:** -
**Type:** QROC
**Tag:** `Exams, Final 2025`

### Q2361: Describe the light microscopic characteristics of an axon and explain why the axon is acidophilic
**Model Answer:** Microscopic Characteristics: - Uniform, constant caliber throughout its course. - Arises from a pale conical projection of the cell body termed the axon hillock. - Completely lacks rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and free ribosomes (no Nissl bodies). - Contains abundant longitudinally oriented neurofilaments, microtubules, mitochondria, and smooth endoplasmic reticulum. Reason for Acidophilia: Because the axon lacks basophilic Nissl granules (ribosomal RNA) and possesses a high concentration of basic cytoskeletal proteins (neurofilament and tubulin proteins), it stains intensely with acidic eosin dyes, appearing uniformly eosinophilic/acidophilic in sharp contrast to the basophilic perikaryon
**Correct Answer:** -

### Q2362: Enumerate the histological layers of the cornea from anterior to posterior
**Model Answer:** 1. Anterior Corneal Epithelium: Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (5-6 cell layers) supported by basal lamina. 2. Bowman's Membrane (Anterior Limiting Lamina): Acellular, homogeneous condensation of randomly arranged type I collagen fibrils. 3. Corneal Stroma (Substantia Propria): Makes up ~90% of corneal thickness, composed of highly organized parallel lamellae of uniform type I collagen fibrils embedded in proteoglycan-rich ground substance, with flattened keratocytes. 4. Descemet's Membrane (Posterior Limiting Lamina): Thick, homogeneous, resilient basement membrane of corneal endothelium composed of type IV and VIII collagen. 5. Corneal Endothelium: Monolayer of simple cuboidal/hexagonal cells possessing active Na+/K+ ATPase pumps responsible for corneal dehydration and deturgescence

### Q2365: Explain why carbamazepine can cause hyponatremia
**Model Answer:** Carbamazepine induces a Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)-like state. It stimulates hypothalamic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH / vasopressin) and enhances the sensitivity and responsiveness of renal collecting duct V2 receptors to circulating ADH. This promotes excessive insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels, causing inappropriate renal water reabsorption, volume expansion, and dilutional hyponatremia
**Correct Answer:** -
